body:
`theme:sector-amc-capital-markets` · confidence: single-source · tickers: HDFCAMC, NAM-INDIA, UTIAMC, BSE, CDSL, MCX, CAMS, KFINTECH, ANGELONE

**How it makes money:** AUM x yield (AMC); volume x fee (exchanges); accounts/transactions (depositories); AUM serviced (RTA).

**Metrics that matter:**
- Equity QAAUM market share
- SIP flows & SIP book
- blended yield (bps) / TER
- net flows
- operating margin
- Exchanges: ADTV, options premium share
- Depository: new demat accounts, active accounts

**Value chain and where margins sit:** Investor -> distributor/broker/platform -> AMC -> RTA -> custodian -> exchange/clearing -> depository. Margins are highest at monopoly infrastructure (depository, exchange); distributors are squeezed by direct plans and discount brokers.

**Cycle drivers:** Market levels and retail sentiment, SEBI fee/TER and F&O rules, STT changes (futures 0.05%, options 0.15% from Apr 2026), IPO/QIP cycle.

**Lead indicators (public India data):**
- AMFI monthly note (AUM, SIP, folios)
- NSE/BSE monthly business growth (F&O premium turnover)
- CDSL/NSDL monthly accounts
- SEBI board meeting agendas & consultation papers
- Primary market pipeline (SEBI DRHP filings)

**What separated winners from losers:** Winners: monopoly/duopoly rails, diversified revenue (not just F&O), strong fund performance and brand, low-cost digital distribution. Losers: discount brokers when retail F&O was curbed (2024–25), AMCs with a long underperformance streak, single-product exchanges.

**Valuation ranges and peaks/troughs:** AMC 25–45x P/E (peaks ~2017–18, 2021, 2024). Exchanges/depositories 40–80x at peaks (CDSL/BSE 2021, 2024). Troughs after SEBI TER cuts (2018) and F&O curbs (late 2024).

**Current state (Nov 2026):** Oct 2026 MF AUM ~₹83.39 lakh cr (+0.9% MoM); equity net inflows ₹32,994 cr (−14% MoM); SIP ₹32,160 cr (third month >₹32k cr); folios 28.78 cr. Total net inflows ~₹1.74 lakh cr, debt-led (AMFI).

**Classic traps:**
- Annualising peak-month volumes
- One SEBI circular can cut a revenue line 30–50%
- Mark-to-market AUM gains in a bull market seen as 'flows'
- Brokers' float income reverses with rate cuts

`person:stanley-druckenmiller` | confidence: **verified** | tags: us, global, process, macro, position-sizing

Duquesne Capital 1981-2010: ~30% average annual return, widely reported as no losing year, though some reports say 2010 (closing year) was down ~5%; returns never publicly audited, so treat as press-reported. Lead PM of Soros's Quantum Fund 1988-2000. Structural edge: in the Soros seat he could deploy multi-billion positions in currencies, bonds and stocks with leverage. Process edge: markets are driven by liquidity (central banks, credit), not earnings; he looks 18-24 months ahead; he sizes very large when conviction and risk/reward line up and cuts fast when wrong ('it's not whether you're right or wrong, but how much you make when right'). Signature trade: Sept 1992 short of sterling before ERM exit (~$1bn, Wikipedia puts Quantum gain at ~$1.8bn for the week). Biggest mistake: 1999-2000 he shorted tech, gave up, then bought ~$6bn of tech near the March 2000 top (unverified figure) and Quantum lost heavily; he left in April 2000. He also says he sold Nvidia too early in 2024. Copyable for an individual: track RBI/Fed liquidity and credit spreads as the master variable; make few large bets, not many small ones; exit as soon as the thesis breaks; when a regime changes, change your mind without ego. Not copyable: leverage, FX/bond access, information flow.

| key | value |
|---|---|
| edge_structural | multi-asset leverage, scale, macro information network |
| edge_process | liquidity first, 18-24m horizon, concentrated sizing, fast cuts |
| signature_trades | GBP short 1992 (~$1bn+); avoided 2008; tech round-trip 2000 (loss) |
| track_record | ~30%/yr 1981/86-2010 (press, unaudited) |
| mistakes | bought tech at 2000 top; sold Nvidia early (2024) |
| copyable | liquidity dashboard, concentration with stop discipline |

body:
**Gap found: solvency.** 15 of 15 leverage blow-ups (Jet, IL&FS, Adani Enterprises, Future, Zee, Unitech, Suzlon-2008,
Kingfisher, SVB, Lehman, Evergrande, GE, Credit Suisse, Paytm, PC Jeweller) passed every hard rule. Proposed new
GRADED solvency flags, to be back-tested before use: negative net worth; interest cover < 1.5x for 2 years;
short-term funding of long assets (lenders: ALM 1-year gap, CP share); dividends or buybacks exceeding FCF while
borrowing; group-level promoter debt (pledge + holdco loans).

**Proposed revised filter set (separate record insight:disqualifiers-v2-proposal; insight:disqualifiers is
unchanged until the user agrees):**
- **HARD at entry (no override):** H1a fake-cash signals · H1b implausible economics *after a written peer/unit-
  economics check* · H1c unverifiable profits · H4 pump patterns (incl. pre-revenue SPAC/IPO hype) · H5 RPT cash
  leakage · H2 auditor exit citing disagreement/denied information or qualified/adverse opinion · H3 rating "not
  cooperating" (unproven, cheap).
- **HARD at exit (sell / no new money until a new auditor signs clean):** H2 and the strongest H2b events (RBI NPA
  divergence, 8-K 4.02 non-reliance, results delayed past the deadline).
- **GRADED (override template):** pledge (>25%; escalate >50% or rising), H2b events, dilution, debtor days with
  counterparty, the new solvency set.
- **QUESTIONS, not flags (description only):** CFO/PAT, negative FCF, debt with negative CFO, other-income share.
- **Moved to stage 5:** P/E > 50 / > 2x own median.

**What would change this verdict:** a point-in-time universe with dead companies showing flagged → >50% loss at
≥ 2x base rate (with x3 not above base) at peak-ish snapshots — that would promote pledge > 50% or the
auditor rule to hard. Re-run with the full Screener universe on the Pi (stage 1) at 4 snapshot dates.

body:
Inference as the survivorship check: unit = fiscal quarter; 95% bootstrap CIs resampling quarters (5,000 draws,
seed 1); all events 2018–2025 primary, 2018–21 / 2022–25 shown.
- **H1 (primary).** Per quarter, mean excess of A minus mean excess of B (quarters where A and B each have ≥ 3 events);
  mean across quarters ≤ **−2.0 pp** and the bootstrap CI upper bound < 0 ⇒ **SUPPORTED**. CI excluding 0 but
  |effect| < 2 pp ⇒ "weaker than hypothesised (real but < 2 pp)". Otherwise **NOT SUPPORTED**.
- **H2 (primary).** Pooled event-level P(halving within 12 months) of A ÷ that of D; quarter-bootstrap CI (resample
  quarters, recompute both pooled rates). Ratio ≥ **2.0** and CI lower bound > 1 ⇒ **SUPPORTED**; CI lower bound > 1
  but ratio < 2 ⇒ "weaker than hypothesised"; otherwise **NOT SUPPORTED**.
- Reported alongside (do not decide H1/H2): A, B, C, D mean excess and P(halving) with CIs; A vs C (is it the miss or
  the flag?); the interaction (A − B) − (C − D); components B25 / B50 / S2 / S5 alone in place of RED; sub-periods;
  LIVE-only events; unknown-as-unflagged; financials excluded.
- **How the decision card uses it (rule fixed now):**
  - H1 supported → the avoid gate escalates: bottom-two SUE **with** a red flag = "EXIT / no entry for ≥ 63 trading
    days, re-check only after the next result"; bottom-two without a flag stays the current WAIT.
  - H1 not supported but H2 supported → the combination is a **tail-risk** rule: keep WAIT as is, but a bottom-two
    result with a red flag caps the position at the minimum size / blocks new money (survival, not drift).
  - Neither → no interaction rule; the PEAD gate and the stage-2 flags stay separate and additive (no new gate).
- Known biases stated in advance: (1) stale pledge (annual June-quarter SHP); (2) firms with no BSE code or no XBRL SHP
  are unknown (NSE-only firms; dead firms that stopped filing) — may hide the worst cases; (3) restated standalone
  annual data; (4) the event set already drops firms below ₹500 cr, where most failures sit (L31), so halving events
  are rarer than in the solvency panel; (5) weekly closes; price returns only; (6) dead firms are a 39% sample.

body:
- **Valuation timing matters.** Since 2004, every negative 5-year Nifty return started at P/E ≥ 24.5;
  starting below P/E 12 gave ~29%/yr.
- **Indian winners mostly grew profits;** only ~37% of the median gain came from a higher P/E. Stocks
  that ended their run at P/E 70+ are mostly lower today (median −48%).
- **Small caps fall >20% about every 2 years** and spent 36% of days (2004–26) >30% below their peak.
- **Tone isn't an edge in India** — optimistic concall language moves prices short-term but doesn't
  predict results. Checking promises vs delivery is the edge.
- **Never trust a company's own "no pledge" statement** — check the exchange data.
